seedDecisions.rationale: This states Craig's Kalam inference from a beginning to a transcendent, uncaused, timeless, spaceless, and immaterial cause, making it indispensable to his cosmological route.
The contrast between culturally transmitted religion and openly tested science supplies an important part of Millican's positive epistemic case for skepticism about religious belief-forming methods.
This directly challenges the causal premise of Craig's Kalam argument by distinguishing observed material rearrangement from creation ex nihilo.
Craig directly answers Millican's religious-diversity and method-reliability argument by denying a single common religious method and identifying his own method as logic, evidence, and experience.
This is Millican's principal probability, sample-size, deeper-physics, and multiverse challenge to Craig's fine-tuning inference.
Craig directly undercuts Millican's expectation-based objection by arguing that evidence against God requires a justified prediction that God would provide more or clearer evidence.
This presents Millican's principal contrary-evidence argument: the observed world and purported divine morality conflict with expectations for a morally perfect God and support skepticism.
Craig directly answers the evil-based evidential argument by proposing that an evil-containing world may serve God's purpose of maximizing freely chosen relationship and salvation.

additions.speaker: William Lane Craig
additions.proposition: Craig's cumulative case will offer five philosophical, scientific, moral, historical, and experiential reasons for theism while maintaining that no comparably good reasons support atheism.
additions.attributionBasis: The continuous span begins Craig's uninterrupted opening case immediately after his introductory remarks and before his first cosmological argument.
additions.rationale: This supplies the explicit cumulative framework connecting Craig's individual evidential lines to his overall comparative conclusion.

additions.speaker: William Lane Craig
additions.proposition: Subtractions from an actually infinite collection yield incompatible results in the real world, so an actual infinite cannot exist and the series of past events must be finite.
additions.attributionBasis: The span is a continuous portion of Craig's opening cosmological argument, from his infinite-coins example through its conclusion about the finite past.
additions.rationale: This is Craig's principal philosophical support for the premise that the universe began to exist.

additions.speaker: William Lane Craig
additions.proposition: The Borde-Guth-Vilenkin result implies a past boundary for any universe with average expansion and applies independently of an early-universe physical description, including to an expanding multiverse.
additions.attributionBasis: The continuous caption span remains within Craig's opening cosmology presentation and follows directly after his philosophical finite-past argument.
additions.rationale: This is Craig's independent scientific support for the universe's finite beginning and was extensively contested later.

additions.speaker: William Lane Craig
additions.proposition: Life-permitting conditions are extraordinarily improbable, are not fixed by physical necessity, and instantiate an independently specified pattern, so design is a better explanation than necessity or chance.
additions.attributionBasis: The span is a continuous segment of Craig's numbered fine-tuning argument, ending with his express inference to a cosmic designer.
additions.rationale: This captures the design inference required for Craig's fine-tuning evidential line.

additions.speaker: William Lane Craig
additions.proposition: Moral experience justifies belief in objective moral values more strongly than skeptical premises undermine it, and because such binding values require God, their existence entails that God exists.
additions.attributionBasis: The span is within Craig's uninterrupted opening moral argument and runs through his explicit conclusion that God exists.
additions.rationale: This preserves the positive moral-evidence line included in Craig's five-part cumulative case.

additions.speaker: William Lane Craig
additions.proposition: The empty-tomb tradition, post-mortem appearances, and unexpected origin of the disciples' resurrection belief lack a plausible naturalistic explanation and are best explained by God raising Jesus.
additions.attributionBasis: The continuous span occurs in Craig's numbered resurrection argument and includes the empty-tomb reference, appearances, disciples' belief, rejection of naturalistic explanations, and conclusion.
additions.rationale: This represents Craig's historical route from the three claimed facts to Jesus' resurrection and God's existence.

additions.speaker: William Lane Craig
additions.proposition: God can be known immediately through personal experience apart from argument, and sincere seekers who attend to God rather than only external proofs can encounter him as a lived reality.
additions.attributionBasis: The span is Craig's uninterrupted fifth opening point, explicitly introduced as personal experience of God.
additions.rationale: This captures the experiential line expressly included in Craig's cumulative case and later challenged by Millican.

additions.speaker: Peter Millican
additions.proposition: All well-attested intelligence and mental causation depend on physical structures and intermediaries, while no solid evidence supports disembodied intelligence or thought surviving destruction of the brain.
additions.attributionBasis: The span is part of Millican's uninterrupted opening case, after he contrasts the Christian hypothesis with alternative supernatural claims and before his Kalam analysis.
additions.rationale: This directly attacks Craig's inference from a nonphysical cosmic cause to an unembodied mind.

additions.speaker: Peter Millican
additions.proposition: The Borde-Guth-Vilenkin theorem establishes only a beginning to average expansion, not necessarily to the universe, and contracting or loop-quantum models can evade the claimed absolute beginning.
additions.attributionBasis: The continuous span is Millican's opening response to Craig's use of the Borde-Guth-Vilenkin theorem and ends with the proposed prior-contraction alternatives.
additions.rationale: This directly contests Craig's scientific support for a finite cosmic past.

additions.speaker: Peter Millican
additions.proposition: Utilitarian, Kantian, and sentiment-based non-theistic theories can supply moral standards independent of popular belief, so Craig must show both why objectivity requires God and why objective values exist in that sense.
additions.attributionBasis: The span is Millican's uninterrupted opening treatment of Craig's moral argument, from his non-theistic examples through his explicit challenge.
additions.rationale: This is Millican's principal opening answer to the claimed dependence of objective morality on God.

additions.speaker: William Lane Craig
additions.proposition: Prior contraction would produce unstable singularities preventing re-expansion, while the Borde-Guth-Vilenkin theorem does not assume Einsteinian gravity and therefore still supports an absolute cosmic beginning.
additions.attributionBasis: The span is Craig's uninterrupted first rebuttal to Millican's Borde-Guth-Vilenkin objections, following Craig's citation of the fuller Vilenkin context.
additions.rationale: This is Craig's principal answer to Millican's contracting-universe and quantum-gravity qualifications.

additions.speaker: William Lane Craig
additions.proposition: Lacking both a material and an efficient cause would make creation more, not less, metaphysically implausible, and even Hume rejected the claim that something could arise wholly without a cause.
additions.attributionBasis: The continuous span is Craig's first rebuttal immediately after he restates the causal premise and directly identifies Millican's creation-from-nothing objection.
additions.rationale: This directly answers Millican's argument that ordinary material-causal experience cannot support causation of creation ex nihilo.

additions.speaker: Peter Millican
additions.proposition: If apparently fine-tuned constants were physically inexplicable and selected from a wide range of alternatives necessary for complexity, they would naturally invite explanation by a cosmic designer.
additions.attributionBasis: Millican explicitly introduces the uninterrupted span with the words that he would concede this much to the fine-tuning argument.
additions.rationale: This materially narrows Millican's opposition by granting a conditional route from robust fine-tuning to cosmic intelligence.

additions.speaker: Peter Millican
additions.proposition: Fine-tuning does not distinguish a morally perfect Christian God from an equally powerful evil or morally neutral designer and therefore fails to establish the specific divine character Craig needs.
additions.attributionBasis: The span is a continuous portion of Millican's fine-tuning rebuttal, beginning with its alleged mismatch to the Christian God and ending with the omnipotence and omniscience problem.
additions.rationale: This directly attacks the specificity of Craig's inference from cosmic design to the Christian God.

additions.speaker: Peter Millican
additions.proposition: Different results for infinity-minus-infinity are not contradictions but reflect that the corresponding inverse equation has multiple solutions, so subtraction is undefined rather than actual infinity being incoherent.
additions.attributionBasis: The span is Millican's uninterrupted mathematical reply to Craig's infinite-coins example during his rebuttal.
additions.rationale: This directly answers the philosophical argument Craig uses to rule out an infinite past.

additions.speaker: William Lane Craig
additions.proposition: Undefined transfinite subtraction does not remove the real-world absurdity, because removing identical cardinal quantities from identical actual collections would still yield nonidentical remainders.
additions.attributionBasis: The span occurs in Craig's uninterrupted second rebuttal and explicitly restates and answers Millican's transfinite-arithmetic objection.
additions.rationale: This preserves Craig's principal rejoinder defending the actual-infinite argument against Millican's mathematical answer.

additions.speaker: William Lane Craig
additions.proposition: Fine-tuning probabilities can be assessed by comparing possible and life-permitting ranges, while the multiplicity and diversity of fine-tuned parameters make their collective force unlikely to disappear under future physics.
additions.attributionBasis: The continuous span is Craig's second-rebuttal response to Millican's probability and immature-physics objections to fine-tuning.
additions.rationale: This directly answers the main epistemic-caution objections to Craig's fine-tuning inference.

additions.speaker: Peter Millican
additions.proposition: The resurrection accounts are late, non-eyewitness, interested Christian writings; Matthew and Luke are dependent rather than independent, and the Gospels contain significant chronological and theological discrepancies.
additions.attributionBasis: The span is Millican's uninterrupted final rebuttal after he explicitly turns to the resurrection and evaluates the Gospel evidence.
additions.rationale: This is Millican's principal historical-evidential challenge to Craig's resurrection inference.

additions.speaker: Peter Millican
additions.proposition: Religious experience is an unreliable knowledge method shared across conflicting traditions, and resurrection experiences should be tested as potentially natural psychological phenomena rather than treated as self-authenticating.
additions.attributionBasis: The continuous span is the opening of Millican's closing statement, where he expressly answers Craig's claim that religious experience had gone undiscussed.
additions.rationale: This directly challenges Craig's experiential evidence and connects it to a natural psychological alternative.

additions.speaker: William Lane Craig
additions.proposition: Fine-tuning and Craig's other evidential arguments establish at most a being of enormous power, not infinite power; an additional ontological argument would be needed for the latter.
additions.attributionBasis: The span is Craig's immediate answer in the moderated exchange after Millican conditionally grants cosmic intelligence but denies that it is infinite.
additions.rationale: This materially narrows what Craig claims his evidential case establishes and acknowledges a remaining gap to the omnipotence of the Christian God.

bridgeCoverage.rationale: Craig explicitly frames a five-line comparative case, and the selected cosmological, fine-tuning, moral, resurrection, and experiential moves supply each component of that stated route.
The cumulative framework and its five selected evidential lines represent Craig's claimed convergence for theism over atheism.
The philosophical finite-past argument, scientific beginning argument, and inference to a transcendent cause jointly express this cosmological route.
Craig expressly rejects necessity and chance and infers a cosmic designer from life-permitting fine-tuning.
Craig links the empty tomb, appearances, and origin of resurrection belief to the conclusion that God raised Jesus.
Millican expressly concludes that the evidence strongly favors skepticism and supplies very little support for God.
The selected moves jointly present Millican's underdetermination, method-reliability, natural-alternative, specificity, and contrary-evidence objections across Craig's five lines.
Millican disputes both the causal extrapolation from ordinary material changes and the scientific claim that the universe itself had an absolute beginning.
Millican identifies uncertain cosmic probabilities, deeper-physics and multiverse alternatives, and the failure of design evidence to identify the morally perfect Christian God.
Millican expressly argues that the observed world's evil and purported divine morality are less expected from a perfect God and support skepticism.

materialConcessionAudit.rationale: Craig explicitly concedes that his evidential arguments do not establish infinite power and would require an additional argument to reach that attribute.
Millican explicitly grants that sufficiently robust and physically inexplicable fine-tuning would naturally invite a cosmic-designer explanation.
